entities.name: Roman Senate
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Roman Senate (Latin: Senatus Romanus) — the governing council of the Roman Republic and a significant institution throughout the Roman Empire — was one of the most consequential legislative and advisory bodies in world history, operating continuously in various forms for approximately 1,200 years (from the legendary founding of Rome in 753 BCE through the Eastern Roman Empire's continuation), and serving as the foundational model for parliamentary governance, the concept of a deliberative legislative body, and republican government that has influenced all subsequent democratic institutions.

The Republican Roman Senate (roughly 509-27 BCE) held extraordinary powers: controlling state finances and treasury, directing foreign policy and war declarations, ratifying laws, appointing governors, and serving as the supreme advisory body to the annually elected consuls. The Senate's composition of approximately 300-600 former magistrates (ex-consuls, ex-praetors, etc.) created a de facto oligarchic system dominated by the aristocratic class (patricians and subsequently wealthy plebeians) that limited popular democratic participation while maintaining collective governance.

The Senate's historical arc encapsulates Rome's constitutional history: from the Republic's Senate dominating Roman governance (the Senate's acronym SPQR — Senatus Populusque Romanus, 'Senate and People of Rome' — emblazoned on Roman standards), through the Republic's fall under Julius Caesar and Augustus (who maintained the Senate as an institution while draining it of real power), to the Empire's Senate as largely ceremonial but maintaining symbolic legitimacy, to the late Empire period when the Senate's authority collapsed with Rome's political crisis.
